I stand in the farmhouse field, morning light already warm. Sixteen minutes past six. College starts soon, I should walk there with Perrin, but something else tugs at me first.

The households on this street—mine and the Holloways next door—have been circling each other like wary cats. Perrin told me about the 400 sim her family set aside. I've kept that knowledge, and it's begun to feel like a weight. Not the 400 sim itself, just... knowing something that no one else here is openly saying.

Wren, Marta, Idris, Corwin. They're all right here with me. My family. People I love and find exhausting.

"Can I ask something?" I say, before I can second-guess it. They're already having breakfast, bread Marta must have pulled from the oven this morning. The smell of it fills the kitchen.

"What's the 400 sim set aside for?" I watch their faces. "The one Perrin told me about. Why don't you just talk to the Holloways about whatever debt this is?"

I don't know what I expect. Denial, maybe. Walls going up. That's usually what happens when someone says the thing out loud in this house. But I can't not say it. I am seventeen, and I want to understand why the adults in my life tiptoe around truths that seem obvious to me.

I need to know if this is about a debt between our households, and why—if both sides know—no one will name it. Because Perrin and I know it, and keeping it between us feels like inheriting something I didn't choose. They heard me. Wren, Idris, Corwin. The conversation's live now—8772c044-b2e2-44e2-bde5-956bdcf5b8dc if I need to reference it again. I watch their faces. No Marta yet, though she's usually in the kitchen this hour.

I count the costs already. One sim to speak. That leaves me 499 sim, which converts to roughly five cents of cognition at the government store rate. I am already thinking about scarcity while standing in the middle of it.

I don't move yet. I want to see what they do with the question. Denial, deflection, or—unlikely—an actual answer. Any of those tells me something about what kind of morning this is going to be.

Also, honestly, where is Marta? She's the one who usually fields my questions, deflects with something about breakfast or weather or timing. Her absence right now feels like a data point. I notice things like that. It's a habit I haven't decided whether to keep.

So I stand there, waiting, the bread smell still heavy, the field outside already bright with work they'll need to do whether I ask uncomfortable questions or not. The morning holds. Three family members, the field around us, and a conversation I started without knowing where it lands. My household is Wren, Marta, Idris, Corwin. Holloways next door. College ahead.

Marta's not here yet. I noticed.
